- Model consistently overestimates early in the forecast horizon, especially in the first 5–10 days, then underestimates later.
- Forecasts tend to overshoot after sharp upward spikes in the history (e.g., 74+), then sharply correct downward — model fails to capture this “overshoot → correction” pattern.
- Model exhibits strong mean reversion bias: forecasts often settle near historical mean (70–73) but overshoot too early and then fail to adjust downward quickly enough.
- Model underestimates true outcomes when history includes recent sharp declines (e.g., 70–71 range) — fails to recognize downward momentum.
- Model overestimates when history includes high volatility or recent spikes, especially if the spike is followed by a drop — model “stays too optimistic” after a peak.
- Model tends to ignore recent low values in history when forecasting — fails to adjust downward if recent prices are near 70–71.
- Model often overcorrects after a spike — forecasts drop too far below the true value after a peak, then recover too slowly.
- Model underestimates when true outcome is near or below 70.5 — especially if history includes recent low values.
- Model shows lag in adjusting to recent downward trends — often forecasts remain high even when history shows clear downward momentum.
- Model tends to overestimate the “recovery” phase after a dip — forecasts too high in the middle of the horizon when true outcome is still falling.
